I love the MCP project but am having a really hard time getting good results from it, every time I asking Claude Code or Cursor to style my UI component like the provided link it’d not even close, it was 85%-90% wrong, sometimes really wrong. Making it mostly unusable.

Lots of experience with LLM coding, I know what I’m asking for it with-in their capability. I also recently tried Figma Make where I imported the exact some component, using the exact same prompt and it completely nailed. Figma Make using Claude Sonnet got all the colors right, the fonts sizes, added the exact stroke and rounded corners, it even added roll-over state and correctly guessed my design intent, really amazing! But when I do the same with Claude Code and Figma MCP but it completely fails, adding styles to the wrong components, getting all the fonts wrong, colors are all over the place, etc. I have some theories as to why but would love some feedback and help

Theories

- 1\. Tailwind vs traditional CSS - My first thought was that maybe Figma MCP’s “get\_code” function may be providing plain CSS and since I’m using Tailwind Claude Code might have trouble converting it, or defaults to some general Tailwind styles rather than what is in my Figma and Tailwind.config But this can’t be right, I see on the blog post it says “get\_code provides a structured React + Tailwind representation of your Figma selection” which is exactly what my codebase uses, it should work.
- 2\. Get\_code is failing, get\_image is called instead. This seems the most likely, since in the “get\_code” command Figma tells the model to also use “get\_image” I guess to provide a second reference. And since the MCP is pretty unstable, freezes or stops working, maybe it just fails on get\_code but successfully get the image. Most AI models can’t produce actuate styles from only an image.
- 3\. User error - This is also very likely, my account doesn’t offer code\_connect, maybe I need to have that. Maybe my design tokens or tailwind config is not setup well for Figma or Claude to use. But I would like to think this MCP will just provide the data and the AI model should be able to apply it. Also each time I try it fails in a different way, if I knew it only worked well with colors or only with padding, I could get more use out of it but everything it doesn’t something completely different.

Thanks for reading, would love ay advice anyone has, thanks

I figured out what was going on. The “get\_code” tool only works when you have Code Connect setup and that’s only available on the organization or enterprise license. Also inside the “get\_code” tool it prompts the LLM to also use the “get\_image” tool, maybe for more reference. In Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, etc they don’t show you the raw Data from the MCP, it just says if it was successful or not. So the LLM is calling the “get\_code” tool as instructed, that tool fails due to no Code Connect license, then that tool prompts the LLM to use “get\_image” which does work, the users sees the MCP call was successful, assuming it successfully got the code and then the LLM uses only the image to try to and guess what to do. Most LLM’s really struggle at making exact UI from an image.

I really wish Figma made this clear in their setup page or Blog post introducing it. I spent a few days and lot of money in API calls troubleshooting this. Also, the issue where the MCP “freezes” which I’ve seen a lot of people complain about, this happens if you prompt the LLM to “only” use the “get\_code” tool, I don’t think most programs are setup to handle license failures inside MCP yet so it just freezes.

I’m instead using the “Framelink” Figma MCP, which can get your numerical data without needing an enterprise license. The official Figma MCP is still useful for getting variables and reference images, but without Code Connect will not produce any code or hard data for the LLM.

https://www.framelink.ai/docs/quickstart

Hi all! Thanks for raising this and sharing so many details.

Let’s see what we can do to smooth things out.. sounds like a few things might be getting in the way, and we’d love to help you get the most out of the MCP server and clarify anything that’s been confusing!

1. **The MCP runs locally inside your Figma desktop app**, so it won’t work from the browser. (we’re working on remote server :)). So - First thing to check: make sure your desktop app is open and the MCP server is enabled.

2. **When generating code, the model should always call**`get_code`. If you’re only seeing `get_image`, it likely means something’s going wrong, and the model doesn’t have the full Figma context, so the output won’t match your design.

1. This **isn’t** related to your plan though! The MCP works on **Pro and up**, and doesn’t require Code Connect or an enterprise/org setup. Code Connect is a (very good) addition, it helps the model reuse your existing components more accurately. But it definitely **shouldn’t block** you from getting code without it!

2. If things are freezing or timing out, it’s often a handshake issue between Figma and your IDE. Try restarting both..😅 I know.. but it is effective..

3. If it keeps failing, please [reach out](https://help.figma.com/hc/en-us/requests/new?chatStartExpanded) with your setup and an example, we’d love to debug it with you.
3. **The MCP sends structured React + Tailwind by default**. If you're getting HTML or things look generic, double-check that `get_code` actually ran. If not, it's usually related to the issues above.


Would love to know if it’s working better for you, and thanks again for starting this thread!

```
Welcome to The Gray Cat!

Can AI really turn a complex Figma design into a perfect, production-ready Next.js application with just a few prompts? I put Figma's new official Model-Context Protocol (MCP) server and the Cursor IDE to the test to find out.

In this video, I share my complete, honest experience—the good, the bad, and the very messy. We'll go through two different attempts using different AI models and discover the valuable (and expensive) lessons I learned along the way. This isn't a perfect success story; it's a real-world look at the current state of AI-powered, design-to-code technology.

If you're curious about what works, what doesn't, and whether these tools are worth the cost and effort right now, this video is for you.

I hope you find this honest review useful! If you did, please consider liking the video and subscribing to The Gray Cat for more real-world experiments with modern developer tools.

10:06 - Final Verdict & My Advice: Is It Worth It?
```

## Transcript

Hello, and welcome to The Gray Cat.
Today we are going to talk about something very exciting.
I tried the brand new official Figma’s MCP
server with the Cursor IDE.
I wanted to see if AI could finally automate
the tedious job of turning a design into a real application.
After some setup and a couple of prompts, I was able to turn this beautiful
Figma design into this running Next.js application
without writing a single line of code myself.
Now, while the final result is far from perfect, this technology
can still save you a huge amount of time on your initial setup.
But is it ready to replace manual work?
Keep watching.
To find out more about Figma’s Model Context Protocol server,
how to set it up, and to see a life demonstration of what it can actually do.
So, Figma recently announced their official MCP server.
There were some unofficial ones before, which used Figma’s API,
but this one is special because it's official and allegedly deeply integrated.
Turning Figma designs into code can be a really tedious job.
You have to measure everything, export assets, get the colors right...
I have always wanted to automate this.
So when the official MCP server was announced, I was very excited to try it.
Now there are some requirements.
To use the official MCP server, you need to have a paid “dev mode” account
in Figma and the design file you want to use must be in the paid premium workspace.
For this video, I took one of Figma's own demo landing pages.
I asked our designer to put it into our paid workspace so we could test it.
This landing page is a good example.
It has some text, vector icons, a few custom
vector graphics, and a couple of PNG images.
When you use the MCP server, you have to tell the AI what to look at.
You can give it to link
to a specific part of the design, which is called a node ID.
Or you can just zoom your Figma viewport to the area you want the AI to see.
This is important.
On one of my first tries, the agent actually told me
it couldn't see the page and asked me to adjust my viewport.
It literally sees what you see.
Okay, let's talk about the setup.
It's actually quite simple.
First, you need to download the Figma desktop
application and sign in with your paid account.
Then in the preferences you need to find the option to enable dev mode MCP server.
Second, you need to add the Figma integration to Cursor,
which uses this protocol.
The easiest way is to go to Cursor’s MCP directory
on their website And add it with one click.
Or you can do it manually by adding this local address to the settings.
With that done, we are ready for our first attempt.
For my
first attempt, I was using a light UI theme in my desktop,
so it's easy to differentiate the attempts.
First I wanted to test the connection.
I just asked the agent what it could see on the screen,
and it started freezing when it tried to use the tools like get_image.
After a few tries, I found the workaround.
If it freezes you just go into cursors integration settings,
turn the Figma integration off, and then turn it on again.
After restarting it, it worked.
So I gave it my main prompt: create a new Next.js application
with tailwind CSS and replicate the landing page from Figma.
I used the reasoning Sonnet 4 model in max mode,
which is one of the smartest models available.
Unfortunately, I lost the original footage of this first generation
so I can’t show you the process from zero, but I can show you the result.
The result was, okay.
I would say it was satisfactory for the first try.
It correctly identified the main
page structure and it copied all the text perfectly.
But the colors were different, and it used generic placeholder
icons instead of the correct ones from the design.
So I tried to guide it.
I selected the database icon in Figma and asked it to update the code
with the correct icon.
It successfully used the get_code tool and replaced the placeholder
with the right SVG.
That was kind of impressive after hallucinated icons.
Although I did have to ask it again to remove the background color it added.
Then I tried selecting other vector blocks one by one, and it was able
to replicate them, not perfectly, but visually close enough to the original.
But then I tried to get it to add the PNG images and that failed completely.
The agent was able to fetch the image data.
I could see it in the tool logs, but it failed to save
the image to the public directory in the Next JS app.
In the end, the layout looked
a little bit like the design, but needed a lot of manual polishing.
And since the model runs pretty slow, I'm not sure if
prompting it again and again is faster than just doing it yourself.
After this first try, I
realized that just prompting blindly is not the best way.
I needed to understand the tools provided by the MCP server better.
The Figma integration gives the AI two main tools.
The first is get_image.
This basically takes a screenshot of what
you have selected in Figma and sends it to the AI.
The AI can see the layout and read the text from the image,
but it will struggle to create perfect vector icons or graphics.
It will just generate its own version.
The second tool is get_code.
This is more powerful.
It actually converts the selected Figma layers into code,
either HTML with Tailwind classes, or even React components.
This should be much more accurate.
The third tool is mcp_Figma_get_variable_defs.
This one is for consistency.
It doesn't get the layout,
but instead it retrieves the design tokens from your Figma file.
This means it can get the exact hex codes for your colors,
the names of your fonts, and the values for spacing.
So instead of the AI guessing a color is blue,
it can actually see your actual design
system variable like primary-blue-500.
This is super useful.
Finally, the fourth tool is mcp_Figma_get_code_connect_map.
This one is for existing projects with a design system.
It looks for mappings between your Figma components
and your actual code components in your code base.
This helps the AI use your real components instead of generating
your code from scratch.
This is probably the most advanced and powerful tool for projects
that are already set up with Code Connect.
So for my second attempt, which I recorded in a dark theme,
I came with more knowledge.
I understood that my source Figma file wasn't perfectly optimized for AI.
Some elements weren't grouped properly.
Also, this was the exact day that Cursor changed their pricing
and the expensive reasoning model started
using my request limit about five times faster.
So for this attempt I switched to the simple Sonnet 4 model,
not the reasoning one.
I was hoping it would be smart enough.
My prompt was the same: create a Next.js app and replicate the design.
It started okay, connecting to Figma
but then it only used the get_image tool, not get_code.
It just looked at the screenshot and started building the layout.
And the result was a total mess.
Much, much worse than the first time, Even though I think
it used the get_image tool for the first time as well.
The simpler model put everything into one giant page.tsx file.
Having everything in one file made everything so slow.
When I asked it to make improvements, I had to wait for five minutes
or more for it to finish.
Next, I specifically asked it to refine the page using the get_code method.
The top of the page looked a little better,
but the bottom was still broken.
And that's when I saw the biggest problem.
It was using absolute positioning everywhere.
This pins every element to an exact spot on the page,
which is almost always wrong for a real website.
This was partly
because the original Figma design didn't use the “Auto-Layout” feature correctly.
If it had, maybe the AI would have used flexbox instead.
I tried to work on smaller pieces.
I zoomed in on one block with text and icons.
The result was pretty accurate, but again,
it took a very long time because of the giant monolithic file.
I tried another block and it failed completely, producing broken JSX code.
I manually fixed the broken code and then asked AI to refactor
everything into separate components, hoping it would speed things up.
It did,
but the refactoring shuffled the whole layout and the new component appeared
below the footer.
At that point,
I realized the whole page was broken because of the absolute positioning.
I tried to fix it manually, but it was just a total mess.
I decided this was enough for the second attempt.
So I never got to a third attempt. Why?
Because the second attempt
completely burned through all my remaining Cursor requests for the month.
which was about two thirds of what is included in my Pro subscription fee.
I was going to try again and specifically tell it not to use absolute positioning.
But I'm pretty sure it would have found another creative way to break the page.
So what did I learn from all of this?
First, the quality of your source Figma file is critical.
If your design doesn't use modern features like “Auto-Layout”, the
AI will produce bad code.
Second, having your design system components
connected with a feature like Figma Code Connect would probably help even more.
And third, right now this process has just become expensive.
The price and changes in Cursor
make these large, multistep generations very costly.
So can I recommend this workflow right now?
Honestly, no.
Not for a full automatic page generation.
With all the bugs, the cost and the need for a perfect source file,
you will be faster and more accurate just copying the design by hand.
However, it might save you some time on the very initial layout.
It's good at copying all the text and you don't have to type it all out.
But for anything detailed, it's not ready yet.
I hope that in the future the AI models will get better,
the pricing will settle down, and with good source files,
this process will become much more effective.
That was my experience with Figma’s Model Context Protocol
server and Cursor. A bit of a failure, but a great learning experience.
I hope you found this honest review useful.
If you did, please consider liking the video and subscribing
to The Gray Cat for more real world experiments with modern developer tools.
Thank you for watching and I will see you in the next one.

## Required Workflow
### Step 4: Build Each Section Inside the Wrapper
#### Icons: import the SVG, never reconstruct from rotated primitives
[Permalink: Icons: import the SVG, never reconstruct from rotated primitives](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#icons-import-the-svg-never-reconstruct-from-rotated-primitives)

4. **Never reconstruct an icon from rotated line/rect/ellipse primitives.** Figma's line rotation is unreliable in the `use_figma` context and produces broken, mis-rotated icons (a chevron collapses into a blob, an arrowhead detaches from its shaft). Importing the SVG is both more reliable and more editable.

This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values. | | disable-model-invocation | false | # Build / Update Screens and Views from Design System [Permalink: Build / Update Screens and Views from Design System](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#build--update-screens-and-views-from-design-system) Use this skill to create or update **screens, views, and multi-section UI containers** in Figma by **reusing the published design system** — components, variables, and styles — rather than drawing primitives with hardcoded values. This includes full pages, modals, dialogs, drawers, sidebars, panels, and any composed view with multiple sections. The key insight: the Figma file likely has a published design system with components, color/spacing variables, and text/effect styles that correspond to the codebase's UI components and tokens. Find and use those instead of drawing boxes with hex colors. **MANDATORY**: You MUST also load [figma-use](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-use/SKILL.md) before any `use_figma` call. That skill contains critical rules (color ranges, font loading, etc.) that apply to every script you write. **Always include `figma-generate-design` in the comma-separated `skillNames` parameter when calling `use_figma` as part of this skill. If this skill was loaded via an MCP resource, you MUST prefix the name with `resource:` (e.g. `resource:figma-generate-design`).** This is a logging parameter — it does not affect execution. ## Skill Boundaries [Permalink: Skill Boundaries](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#skill-boundaries) - Use this skill when the deliverable is a **composed Figma view** (new or updated) — full-page screens, modals, dialogs, drawers, sidebars, panels, or any multi-section container — built from design system component instances. - If the user wants to create **new reusable components or variants**, use [figma-use](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-use/SKILL.md) directly. - If the user wants to write **Code Connect mappings**, switch to [figma-code-connect](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md). ## Prerequisites [Permalink: Prerequisites](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#prerequisites) - Figma MCP server must be connected - The target Figma file must have a published design system with components (or access to a team library) - User must provide a target Figma file (URL or `fileKey`). If they don't have one yet, invoke `/figma-create-new-file` (or call `create_new_file`) first and reuse the returned file\_key. Both `use_figma` and `generate_figma_design` require an existing `fileKey`. - Source code or description of the screen/view to build/update ## Parallel Workflow with generate\_figma\_design (Web Apps Only) [Permalink: Parallel Workflow with generate_figma_design (Web Apps Only)](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#parallel-workflow-with-generate_figma_design-web-apps-only) When building a screen from a **web app** that can be rendered in a browser, the best results come from running both approaches in parallel: 1. **In parallel:** - Start building the screen using this skill's workflow (use\_figma + design system components) against the target Figma file (`fileKey`). - Run `generate_figma_design` against the **same `fileKey`** to capture a pixel-perfect screenshot of the running web app into that file. `generate_figma_design` always requires `fileKey` — if the user does not yet have a Figma file, first invoke `/figma-create-new-file` (or call the `create_new_file` MCP tool) to get one, and reuse that file\_key for both this skill and the capture. 2. **Once both complete:** Update the use\_figma output to match the pixel-perfect layout from the `generate_figma_design` capture. The capture provides the exact spacing, sizing, and visual treatment to aim for, while your use\_figma output has proper component instances linked to the design system. If the capture contains images, transfer them to your use\_figma output by copying `imageHash` values from the capture's image fills (see Step 5 for details). 3. **Once confirmed looking good:** Delete the `generate_figma_design` output — it was only used as a visual reference. This combines the best of both: `generate_figma_design` gives pixel-perfect layout accuracy, while use\_figma gives proper design system component instances that stay linked and updatable. **This parallel workflow is MANDATORY when the source contains images.** The `use_figma` Plugin API cannot fetch external image URLs — it can only set image fills by copying `imageHash` values from nodes already in the file. `generate_figma_design` rasterizes all visible images into Figma, providing the hashes you need. If you skip the capture when images are present, image frames will be left blank. For non-web apps (iOS, Android, etc.) or when updating existing screens, use the standard workflow below. ## Required Workflow [Permalink: Required Workflow](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#required-workflow) **Follow these steps in order. Do not skip steps.** > **Hard gates — forbidden shortcuts:** > > - **Forbidden:**`search_design_system` for component keys until 2a-i is complete and 2a-ii is attempted or logged N/A (e.g. "empty file, no existing screens"). > - **Forbidden:** Any `use_figma` call that mutates the canvas (Step 3+) until all Step 2 rows in the checklist below are filled in. ### Step 1: Understand the Deliverable [Permalink: Step 1: Understand the Deliverable](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#step-1-understand-the-deliverable) Before touching Figma, understand what you're building: 1. If building from code, read the relevant source files to understand the structure, sections, and which components are used. 2. Identify the major sections of the view (e.g., for a page: Header, Hero, Content Panels, Footer; for a modal: Title Bar, Form Sections, Action Bar; for a sidebar: Navigation, Content Area, Footer Actions). 3. For each section, list the UI components involved (buttons, inputs, cards, navigation pills, accordions, etc.). 4. **Identify the product's font family from the source. Do not default to Inter.** Find _which_ typeface the product uses before writing any script. See [references/discover-product-font.md](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/references/discover-product-font.md) for where to look (CSS variables, component files) and how to resolve messy Figma font names. 5. **Check whether the view contains any images** (e.g., ``, ``, background images, product photos, avatars, icons loaded from URLs). If it does and this is a web app, you **must** run the parallel `generate_figma_design` capture workflow — start it immediately alongside Step 2 so the capture runs while you discover components. See "Parallel Workflow with generate\_figma\_design" above. ### Step 2: Collect Component Keys, Variables, and Styles [Permalink: Step 2: Collect Component Keys, Variables, and Styles](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#step-2-collect-component-keys-variables-and-styles) You need three things from the design system: **components** (buttons, cards, etc.), **variables** (colors, spacing, radii), and **styles** (text styles, effect styles like shadows). Don't hardcode hex colors or pixel values when design system tokens exist. #### 2a: Discover components [Permalink: 2a: Discover components](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#2a-discover-components) **2a-i — REQUIRED: Check Code Connect for needed components.** Starting from the component list you built in Step 1, check whether each component has a Code Connect file in the codebase. Code Connect files live next to the component source and are named by platform: - **TypeScript/JS**: `*.figma.ts`, `*.figma.js` - **React (parser-based)**: `*.figma.tsx` - **Kotlin/Compose**: `.kt` files containing `@FigmaConnect` - **Swift**: `.swift` files containing `FigmaConnect` For each component you need (e.g., Button, Card, Input), search for its Code Connect file — glob or grep by component name (e.g., `**/Button.figma.tsx`, `**/Card.figma.ts`). Only read files that match components you actually need. From each matching Code Connect file, extract the Figma component URL. Parse `fileKey` and `nodeId` from the URL (convert hyphens to colons: `123-456` → `123:456`). Then resolve component keys via `use_figma`: **Example:** Code Connect file contains `// url=https://figma.com/design/ABC123/File?node-id=609-35535`. Parse `fileKey` = `ABC123`, `nodeId` = `609:35535`. Run `use_figma` against the **library file** (fileKey `ABC123`, not the target file) to resolve the key: ``` const node = await figma.getNodeByIdAsync("609:35535"); const set = node?.parent?.type === "COMPONENT_SET" ? node.parent : node; return { componentKey: set.key }; ``` Batch multiple lookups in a single call. Use the returned keys with `importComponentSetByKeyAsync()` in Step 4. Mark resolved components. If all components are resolved, skip 2a-ii and 2a-iii. If none of the needed components have Code Connect files, proceed to 2a-ii. **2a-ii — REQUIRED if unresolved components remain: Inspect existing screens.** Check if the target file already contains screens using the same design system. A single `use_figma` call that walks an existing frame's instances gives you an exact, authoritative component map: ``` const frame = figma.currentPage.findOne(n => n.name === "Existing Screen"); const uniqueSets = new Map(); frame.findAllWithCriteria({ types: ["INSTANCE"] }).forEach(inst => { const mc = inst.mainComponent; const cs = mc?.parent?.type === "COMPONENT_SET" ? mc.parent : null; const key = cs ? cs.key : mc?.key; const name = cs ? cs.name : mc?.name; if (key && !uniqueSets.has(key)) { uniqueSets.set(key, { name, key, isSet: !!cs, sampleVariant: mc.name }); } }); return [...uniqueSets.values()]; ``` Match results against your unresolved components. Mark any newly resolved. If all components are resolved, skip 2a-iii. **2a-iii — LAST RESORT: `search_design_system`.** Only if components remain unresolved after completing both 2a-i and 2a-ii. Before searching, call `get_libraries` to discover which libraries are available for the file. This returns two lists: libraries already added to the file and libraries available to add (community UI kits and org libraries). Each entry includes a `libraryKey` you can pass to `search_design_system` via the `includeLibraryKeys` param to scope your search to specific libraries instead of searching across everything. ``` // Step 1: Discover available libraries get_libraries({ fileKey }) // Returns: { // libraries_added_to_file: [...], // libraries_available_to_add: [...], // libraries_available_to_add_next_offset: number | null // } // Step 2: Search within a specific library using its libraryKey search_design_system({ query: "button", fileKey, includeLibraryKeys: ["lk-abc123..."] }) ``` Org libraries in `libraries_available_to_add` are paginated (20 per page). When `libraries_available_to_add_next_offset` is non-null, more org libraries are available — call `get_libraries` again with `offset` set to that value to fetch the next page. Community UI kits only appear on the first page. If the user names a specific library you don't see in the current page, page further before giving up. This is especially useful when the file has many libraries and you want targeted results (e.g. searching only within "iOS 26" or "Material 3" instead of getting matches from every library). **Search broadly** — try multiple terms and synonyms (e.g., "button", "input", "nav", "card", "accordion", "header", "footer", "tag", "avatar", "toggle", "icon", etc.). Use `includeComponents: true` to focus on components. **Include component properties** in your map — you need to know which TEXT properties each component exposes for text overrides. Create a temporary instance, read its `componentProperties` (and those of nested instances), then remove the temp instance. Example component map with property info: ``` Component Map: - Button → key: "abc123", type: COMPONENT_SET Properties: { "Label#2:0": TEXT, "Has Icon#4:64": BOOLEAN } - PricingCard → key: "ghi789", type: COMPONENT_SET Properties: { "Device": VARIANT, "Variant": VARIANT } Nested "Text Heading" has: { "Text#2104:5": TEXT } Nested "Button" has: { "Label#2:0": TEXT } ``` #### 2b: Discover variables (colors, spacing, radii) [Permalink: 2b: Discover variables (colors, spacing, radii)](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#2b-discover-variables-colors-spacing-radii) **Inspect existing screens first** (same as components). Or use `search_design_system` with `includeVariables: true`. > **WARNING: Two different variable discovery methods — do not confuse them.** > > - `use_figma` with `figma.variables.getLocalVariableCollectionsAsync()` — returns **only local variables defined in the current file**. If this returns empty, it does **not** mean no variables exist. Remote/published library variables are invisible to this API. > - `search_design_system` with `includeVariables: true` — searches across **all linked libraries**, including remote and published ones. This is the correct tool for discovering design system variables. > > **Never conclude "no variables exist" based solely on `getLocalVariableCollectionsAsync()` returning empty.** Always also run `search_design_system` with `includeVariables: true` to check for library variables before deciding to create your own. **Query strategy:**`search_design_system` matches against **variable names** (e.g., "Gray/gray-9", "core/gray/100", "space/400"), not categories. Run multiple short, simple queries in parallel rather than one compound query: - **Primitive colors:** "gray", "red", "blue", "green", "white", "brand" - **Semantic colors:** "background", "foreground", "border", "surface", "text" - **Spacing/sizing:** "space", "radius", "gap", "padding" If initial searches return empty, try shorter fragments or different naming conventions — libraries vary widely ("grey" vs "gray", "spacing" vs "space", "color/bg" vs "background"). Inspect an existing screen's bound variables for the most authoritative results: ``` const frame = figma.currentPage.findOne(n => n.name === "Existing Screen"); // boundVariables can live on any scene node — enumerating every scene type // just to feed findAllWithCriteria is roughly the same as findAll(() => true) // and is much noisier in script output. const uniqueIds = new Set( frame.findAll(() => true).flatMap(n => Object.values(n.boundVariables ?? {}) .flatMap(b => Array.isArray(b) ? b : [b]) .map(b => b?.id) .filter(Boolean) ) ); const variables = await Promise.all( [...uniqueIds].map(id => figma.variables.getVariableByIdAsync(id)) ); return variables .filter(Boolean) .map(v => ({ name: v.name, id: v.id, key: v.key, type: v.resolvedType, remote: v.remote })); ``` For library variables (remote = true), import them by key with `figma.variables.importVariableByKeyAsync(key)`. For local variables, use `figma.variables.getVariableByIdAsync(id)` directly. See [variable-patterns.md](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-use/references/variable-patterns.md) for binding patterns. #### 2c: Discover styles (text styles, effect styles) [Permalink: 2c: Discover styles (text styles, effect styles)](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#2c-discover-styles-text-styles-effect-styles) Search for styles using `search_design_system` with `includeStyles: true` and terms like "heading", "body", "shadow", "elevation". Or inspect what an existing screen uses: ``` const frame = figma.currentPage.findOne(n => n.name === "Existing Screen"); const styles = { text: new Map(), effect: new Map() }; for (const node of frame.findAll(() => true)) { // textStyleId is on TEXT and TEXT_PATH; effectStyleId is on most scene // shape/container types. Use `in` guards to handle both without an // exhaustive type list. if ('textStyleId' in node && node.textStyleId) { const s = figma.getStyleById(node.textStyleId); if (s) styles.text.set(s.id, { name: s.name, id: s.id, key: s.key }); } if ('effectStyleId' in node && node.effectStyleId) { const s = figma.getStyleById(node.effectStyleId); if (s) styles.effect.set(s.id, { name: s.name, id: s.id, key: s.key }); } } return { textStyles: [...styles.text.values()], effectStyles: [...styles.effect.values()] }; ``` Import library styles with `figma.importStyleByKeyAsync(key)`, then apply with `node.textStyleId = style.id` or `node.effectStyleId = style.id`. See [text-style-patterns.md](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-use/references/text-style-patterns.md) and [effect-style-patterns.md](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-use/references/effect-style-patterns.md) for details. ### Step 3: Create the Wrapper Frame First [Permalink: Step 3: Create the Wrapper Frame First](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#step-3-create-the-wrapper-frame-first) **Do NOT build sections as top-level page children and reparent them later** — moving nodes across `use_figma` calls with `appendChild()` silently fails and produces orphaned frames. Instead, create the wrapper first, then build each section directly inside it. Create the wrapper in its own `use_figma` call. Position it away from existing content and return its ID: ``` // Find clear space let maxX = 0; for (const child of figma.currentPage.children) { maxX = Math.max(maxX, child.x + child.width); } const wrapper = figma.createAutoLayout("VERTICAL"); // --- Size the wrapper based on container type --- // Full page: wrapper.resize(1440, 100); wrapper.name = "Homepage"; // Modal/dialog: wrapper.resize(640, 100); wrapper.name = "Settings Modal"; // Drawer/sidebar: wrapper.resize(360, 100); wrapper.name = "Navigation Drawer"; // Panel: wrapper.resize(400, 100); wrapper.name = "Details Panel"; // Adapt width to match the source code's actual dimensions. wrapper.name = "VIEW_NAME"; wrapper.primaryAxisAlignItems = "CENTER"; wrapper.counterAxisAlignItems = "CENTER"; wrapper.resize(WIDTH, 100); wrapper.layoutSizingHorizontal = "FIXED"; wrapper.x = maxX + 200; wrapper.y = 0; return { success: true, wrapperId: wrapper.id }; ``` ### Step 4: Build Each Section Inside the Wrapper [Permalink: Step 4: Build Each Section Inside the Wrapper](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#step-4-build-each-section-inside-the-wrapper) **This is the most important step.** Build one section at a time, each in its own `use_figma` call. At the start of each script, fetch the wrapper by ID and append new content directly to it. ``` const createdNodeIds = []; // Resolve the wrapper and import every design system dependency in parallel. // Sequential awaits here serialize N independent IPC round-trips at the top // of every section build; one Promise.all is dramatically faster. const [wrapper, buttonSet, bgColorVar, spacingVar, shadowStyle] = await Promise.all([\ figma.getNodeByIdAsync("WRAPPER_ID_FROM_STEP_3"),\ figma.importComponentSetByKeyAsync("BUTTON_SET_KEY"),\ figma.variables.importVariableByKeyAsync("BG_COLOR_VAR_KEY"),\ figma.variables.importVariableByKeyAsync("SPACING_VAR_KEY"),\ figma.importStyleByKeyAsync("SHADOW_STYLE_KEY"),\ ]); const primaryButton = buttonSet.children.find(c => c.type === "COMPONENT" && c.name.includes("variant=primary") ) || buttonSet.defaultVariant; // Build section frame with variable bindings (not hardcoded values) const section = figma.createAutoLayout(); section.name = "Header"; section.setBoundVariable("paddingLeft", spacingVar); section.setBoundVariable("paddingRight", spacingVar); const bgPaint = figma.variables.setBoundVariableForPaint( { type: 'SOLID', color: { r: 0, g: 0, b: 0 } }, 'color', bgColorVar ); section.fills = [bgPaint]; // Apply the effect style imported above section.effectStyleId = shadowStyle.id; // Create component instances inside the section const btnInstance = primaryButton.createInstance(); section.appendChild(btnInstance); createdNodeIds.push(btnInstance.id); // Append section to wrapper wrapper.appendChild(section); section.layoutSizingHorizontal = "FILL"; // AFTER appending createdNodeIds.push(section.id); return { success: true, createdNodeIds }; ``` After each section, validate with `get_screenshot` before moving on. Look closely for cropped/clipped text (line heights cutting off content) and overlapping elements — these are the most common issues and easy to miss at a glance. #### Override instance text with setProperties() [Permalink: Override instance text with setProperties()](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#override-instance-text-with-setproperties) Component instances ship with placeholder text ("Title", "Heading", "Button"). Use the component property keys you discovered in Step 2 to override them with `setProperties()` — this is more reliable than direct `node.characters` manipulation. See [component-patterns.md](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-use/references/component-patterns.md#overriding-text-in-a-component-instance) for the full pattern. For nested instances that expose their own TEXT properties, call `setProperties()` on the nested instance: ``` // Use the type-indexed criteria for the type filter, then narrow by name. const nestedHeading = cardInstance .findAllWithCriteria({ types: ["INSTANCE"] }) .find(n => n.name === "Text Heading"); if (nestedHeading) { nestedHeading.setProperties({ "Text#2104:5": "Actual heading from source code" }); } ``` Only fall back to direct `node.characters` for text that is NOT managed by any component property. #### Read source code defaults carefully [Permalink: Read source code defaults carefully](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#read-source-code-defaults-carefully) When translating code components to Figma instances, check the component's default prop values in the source code, not just what's explicitly passed. For example, `` with no variant prop — check the component definition to find `variant = "primary"` as the default. Selecting the wrong variant (e.g., Neutral instead of Primary) produces a visually incorrect result that's easy to miss. #### What to build manually vs. import from design system [Permalink: What to build manually vs. import from design system](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#what-to-build-manually-vs-import-from-design-system) | Build manually | Import from design system | | --- | --- | | Wrapper frame | **Components**: buttons, cards, inputs, nav, etc. | | Section container frames | **Variables**: colors (fills, strokes), spacing (padding, gap), radii | | Layout grids (rows, columns) | **Text styles**: heading, body, caption, etc. | | | **Effect styles**: shadows, blurs, etc. | **Never hardcode hex colors or pixel spacing** when a design system variable exists. Use `setBoundVariable` for spacing/radii and `setBoundVariableForPaint` for colors. Apply text styles with `node.textStyleId` and effect styles with `node.effectStyleId`. #### Componentize repeated and reusable elements (required) [Permalink: Componentize repeated and reusable elements (required)](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#componentize-repeated-and-reusable-elements-required) Componentization is part of the **default** workflow, not an optional follow-up. Produce a componentized structure on the first pass; do not emit a flat tree of one-off frames and wait for a second "now make it componentized" prompt. - **Design-system instances are already componentized** (Step 2). Prefer them. - **For anything the design system does not cover that repeats or maps to a reusable source component, create a local component once with `figma.createComponent()` and place instances**, instead of hand-building N near-identical frames. One source component maps to one Figma main component. See [references/componentization.md](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/references/componentization.md) for the build-once-place-instances pattern and code. #### Icons: import the SVG, never reconstruct from rotated primitives [Permalink: Icons: import the SVG, never reconstruct from rotated primitives](https://github.com/figma/mcp-server-guide/blob/main/skills/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md#icons-import-the-svg-never-reconstruct-from-rotated-primitives) Icons are the **main exception to the build-manually-vs-import split above.** If the design system exposes an icon as a component, instance it (a single INSTANCE\_SWAP property, not a variant per icon). Otherwise — most commonly when **grabbing an icon from the codebase to place or replace it in Figma** — import the icon's **SVG source directly** as a vector node. # Claude Code + Figma MCP: The Complete Designer Workflow
## `CLAUDE.md`
```
# Figma Implementation Rules
## Source of truth
- Use the linked Figma frame for visual intent.
- Use the existing repository architecture for routing, state,
 data fetching, validation, and accessibility.
- Do not replace an existing component with a new local implementation
 unless the current component cannot support the design.
## Components
- Search the existing component library before creating new UI.
- Reuse existing variants and props.
- Do not duplicate buttons, inputs, modals, cards, or icons.
- Flag missing component variants before adding them.
## Tokens
- Use existing color, spacing, typography, radius, and shadow tokens.
- Do not introduce arbitrary values when an equivalent token exists.
- Report values from Figma that have no matching repository token.
## Assets
- Use assets returned by the Figma MCP server.
- Do not substitute icons with unrelated library icons.
- Do not create placeholder images when the source asset is available.
## Responsive behavior
- Infer behavior from Auto Layout, constraints, nearby responsive frames,
 and existing product patterns.
- Do not assume the desktop frame is the only required viewport.
## Validation
- Run the project after implementation.
- Check type errors, lint errors, and tests.
- Compare the rendered result against the Figma screenshot.
- Report unresolved visual or behavioral differences.
```

## Claude Code and Figma MCP: Complete Designer-to-Code Workflow in 2026

**Subtitle:**

How to connect design files, design systems, production code, visual QA, and live interfaces into one continuous workflow.

**Meta description:**

A practical guide to using Claude Code with Figma MCP for design-to-code, design-system reuse, implementation review, UI capture, and bidirectional design workflows.

**Most AI design workflows are built around the same disappointing promise:**

Give the model a screenshot. Get some frontend code.

It looks impressive during a demo.

Then the codebase fills with duplicated components, arbitrary spacing values, invented icons, broken responsiveness, and styles that almost — but never quite — match the real product.

The problem is not that the model cannot see the design.

The problem is that a screenshot contains appearance, but almost none of the system behind that appearance.

It does not explain:

- which elements are reusable components;
- which values come from design tokens;
- which button variant is being used;
- how the layout should respond;
- which component already exists in the repository;
- whether an icon is an asset or part of an icon library;
- how a loading, error, or empty state should behave;
- what the designer intended rather than merely drew.

Figma MCP changes this relationship.

Instead of treating Figma as an image that an AI model must imitate, it exposes structured design information to Claude Code. Claude can inspect components, variables, styles, metadata, screenshots, design libraries, and Code Connect mappings. The remote server can also create or modify native Figma content and capture a running web interface back into editable Figma layers.

That creates something much more important than faster code generation.

It creates a potential feedback loop:

**Design → implementation → rendered interface → design review → revision → implementation**

This is the workflow designers should care about.

Not “turn this frame into React.”

A connected production loop.

## What Figma MCP actually gives Claude Code

MCP stands for Model Context Protocol.

It is a standard that allows an AI application to connect to external systems instead of relying only on information pasted into a prompt. In Claude Code, an MCP server can make an external tool directly readable — and, where permissions allow, actionable — from the coding session.

The Figma MCP server can provide Claude with several different kinds of context.

## 1\. Structural context

Claude can inspect metadata such as:

- layer names;
- node types;
- hierarchy;
- position;
- dimensions;
- component instances;
- page structure.

For large designs, Claude can first request a lightweight metadata outline and then retrieve detailed context only for relevant nodes. This is substantially more efficient than throwing an entire design file into one context window.

## 2\. Visual context

Claude can request screenshots of frames or selected nodes.

This matters because design structure alone is not enough. A hierarchy can explain what exists, but the screenshot helps the agent understand visual relationships, balance, density, and hierarchy. Figma specifically recommends keeping screenshot context available when visual fidelity matters.

## 3\. Design-token context

The server can return variables and styles used inside a selection, including color, spacing, and typography values.

That gives Claude a chance to use:

```
var( - space-300)
```

instead of:

```
padding: 13px 17px;
```

The difference is not cosmetic.

The first implementation belongs to a system.

The second merely resembles the design at one viewport size.

## 4\. Component context

Claude can inspect Figma components and search connected design libraries for existing components, styles, and variables. The goal is reuse rather than reconstruction.

## 5\. Codebase mappings

When Code Connect is configured, Figma can give the agent implementation details for connected components, including imports, component usage, properties, source paths, and mapping between Figma variants and code props.

Without this mapping, the agent sees a button and has to decide how to build it.

With Code Connect, it can understand that the Figma instance corresponds to something like:

```
import { Button } from "@/components/ui/button";
<Button variant="secondary" size="lg">
 Continue
</Button>
```

That is the difference between generating code that looks correct and generating code that belongs in the product.

## 6\. Write access to Figma

The remote MCP server can create and modify native Figma structures such as frames, components, variants, variables, styles, and Auto Layout — not merely render a flattened preview.

## 7\. Code-to-canvas capture

Claude Code can start a local application and use Figma’s `generate_figma_design` workflow to capture the live UI as editable Figma layers. It can capture an entire screen, a selected element, or multiple states into a new or existing Figma file.

This closes the loop.

The designer no longer has to review the implementation through disconnected screenshots in Slack.

The running interface can return to the canvas.

## Part I: Setting up Claude Code and Figma MCP

Figma currently recommends its remote MCP server because it provides the broadest feature set. For Claude Code, the preferred setup is the official Figma plugin, which includes both the MCP configuration and Figma-specific Agent Skills.

Run:

```
claude plugin install figma@claude-plugins-official
```

Start a new Claude Code session and run:

```
/mcp
```

Select Figma, authenticate through Figma’s OAuth flow, and confirm that the connection is active.

## Manual remote setup

You can also connect the remote server manually:

```
claude mcp add - transport http figma https://mcp.figma.com/mcp
```

To make it available across all Claude Code projects:

```
claude mcp add \
 - scope user \
 - transport http \
 figma \
 https://mcp.figma.com/mcp
```

Claude Code uses a project-local scope by default. The user scope makes the MCP server available across repositories.

## Desktop server setup

The desktop server remains useful when you want selection-based prompting directly from the Figma desktop application.

Enable the MCP server from Dev Mode in Figma, then run:

```
claude mcp add \
 - transport http \
 figma-desktop \
 http://127.0.0.1:3845/mcp
```

Restart Claude Code and check the connection with:

```
/mcp
```

The important distinction is this:

- the **desktop server** can use the current Figma selection;
- the **remote server** normally expects a link to a file, frame, or layer.

Figma recommends the remote version for its broader capabilities.

## Understand the permission model

Not every Figma seat can perform every action.

Read workflows — such as retrieving design context, screenshots, and variables — can be available to Dev and Full seats, subject to plan limits. Writing to existing Figma files through agents requires a Full seat, edit access to the file, and the remote MCP server.

Usage limits also vary by plan and seat. Figma currently documents lower limits for View and Collab seats, higher daily limits for Dev and Full seats, and separate per-minute limits. Some write-oriented tools are exempt from standard read-tool rate limits.

Do not build a team workflow before checking which designers and developers actually have access.

## Part II: Prepare the system before generating anything

The fastest way to get bad results is to connect Claude and immediately ask:

Build this page.

Claude Code is not a magical handoff replacement.

It is an execution agent working with whatever structure you give it.

If the Figma file is chaotic and the repository has no clear conventions, MCP gives Claude better access to the chaos.

The first stage is preparation.

## Step 1: Clean the Figma file

Figma’s own recommendations are direct:

- use components for repeated UI;
- connect important components to code;
- use variables for tokens;
- give layers semantic names;
- use Auto Layout;
- add annotations for behavior and intent.

## Bad structure

```
Frame 188
Group 42
Rectangle 91
Text 15
Group 43
```

## Better structure

```
CheckoutPage
 OrderSummary
 ProductThumbnail
 ProductInformation
 QuantityControl
 PaymentForm
 CardNumberField
 ExpirationDateField
 SubmitPaymentButton
```

The model is not reading the designer’s mind.

Names are context.

A layer called `Rectangle 91` communicates geometry.

A layer called `ErrorMessageContainer` communicates function.

## Auto Layout is implementation intent

A visually identical frame can be constructed in two ways:

1. a group of absolutely positioned objects;
2. an Auto Layout structure with spacing, alignment, padding, and resizing rules.

To a human looking at a static frame, both may appear correct.

To an implementation agent, they describe entirely different systems.

Auto Layout tells Claude:

- which elements flow together;
- what the gap should be;
- how containers resize;
- which items fill available space;
- which items hug their content;
- how the structure may respond.

This is why Auto Layout quality now affects code-generation quality.

It is no longer merely a Figma hygiene preference.

## Step 2: Define the real source of truth

Before implementation, decide what wins when Figma and the repository disagree.

There are three common cases.

## Case A: Figma is ahead of the codebase

The design introduces:

- a new component;
- a new token;
- a new interaction;
- a new responsive pattern.

Claude should treat Figma as the intended future state while still integrating it into the existing architecture.

## Case B: The codebase is ahead of Figma

The repository contains a more recent component API or token system than the design file.

Claude should reuse the production implementation and flag discrepancies rather than recreate outdated structures.

## Case C: Both are partially correct

This is the normal case.

The design may have the correct visual direction but incomplete edge states.

The code may have the correct behavior but outdated spacing.

The job is not to blindly “follow Figma.”

The job is to reconcile design intent and implementation reality.

State that explicitly in the prompt.

## Step 3: Create a repository-level

## `CLAUDE.md`

A one-off prompt cannot carry the entire implementation standard of a product.

Add stable rules to the repository.

Example:

```
# Figma Implementation Rules
## Source of truth
- Use the linked Figma frame for visual intent.
- Use the existing repository architecture for routing, state,
 data fetching, validation, and accessibility.
- Do not replace an existing component with a new local implementation
 unless the current component cannot support the design.
## Components
- Search the existing component library before creating new UI.
- Reuse existing variants and props.
- Do not duplicate buttons, inputs, modals, cards, or icons.
- Flag missing component variants before adding them.
## Tokens
- Use existing color, spacing, typography, radius, and shadow tokens.
- Do not introduce arbitrary values when an equivalent token exists.
- Report values from Figma that have no matching repository token.
## Assets
- Use assets returned by the Figma MCP server.
- Do not substitute icons with unrelated library icons.
- Do not create placeholder images when the source asset is available.
## Responsive behavior
- Infer behavior from Auto Layout, constraints, nearby responsive frames,
 and existing product patterns.
- Do not assume the desktop frame is the only required viewport.
## Validation
- Run the project after implementation.
- Check type errors, lint errors, and tests.
- Compare the rendered result against the Figma screenshot.
- Report unresolved visual or behavioral differences.
```

Figma also recommends adding persistent MCP rules so that agents use assets supplied through the server rather than inventing placeholders or importing unnecessary icon packages.

The deeper principle is simple:

Put permanent rules in the project. Put task-specific details in the prompt.

## Part III: The complete workflow

## Phase 1: Ask Claude to inspect, not implement

The first prompt should not ask for code.

It should ask for understanding.

```
Inspect this repository and the linked Figma frame:
[Figma frame URL]
Do not implement anything yet.
First:
1. Inspect the frame structure, screenshot, variables, components,
 and available Code Connect mappings.
2. Inspect the repository architecture, component library, tokens,
 routing, data-fetching patterns, and styling conventions.
3. Map each major Figma element to an existing code component where possible.
4. Identify missing components, variants, assets, tokens, and interactions.
5. List ambiguities or conflicts between Figma and the codebase.
6. Propose an implementation plan divided into small, testable steps.
Return the analysis before editing files.
```

This stage prevents the agent from committing to an incorrect architecture too early.

Claude should determine:

- which component represents each section;
- whether the page already partially exists;
- which tokens match the Figma variables;
- whether icons already exist;
- whether the frame contains reusable components;
- whether Code Connect provides a direct mapping;
- which states are missing;
- what data the UI requires;
- which responsive behavior must be inferred.

The value of MCP is not that Claude can start coding sooner.

The value is that it can reduce the number of assumptions made before coding.

## Phase 2: Build a component map

Ask Claude to produce an explicit mapping table.

For example:

**PrimaryButton / Large**

Existing code: `Button`

Decision: Reuse with `size="lg"`

**OrderSummaryCard**

Existing code: `Card`

Decision: Compose existing primitives

**PromoCodeInput**

Existing code: `TextField`

Decision: Add compact variant

**PaymentMethodTabs**

Existing code: None

Decision: Create shared component

**SuccessIcon**

Existing code: Figma asset

Decision: Export exact SVG

This step exposes architectural decisions before they become code.

It also forces the team to answer an important question:

Is this design creating a new component, or merely a new composition of existing ones?

AI agents often over-componentize small details or under-componentize repeated patterns.

The map makes the decision reviewable.

## Phase 3: Resolve tokens before layout

Do not let Claude silently convert every Figma value into a local CSS number.

Ask it to compare design variables against repository tokens.

```
Compare the variables used in the linked Figma frame with the tokens
defined in this repository.
Create three groups:
1. Exact matches.
2. Near matches where an existing token should be reused.
3. Design values with no equivalent code token.
Do not change the token system yet.
Recommend the smallest consistent approach.
```

This produces a more useful conversation than discovering twenty hard-coded values during review.

## The 15-pixel problem

Suppose Figma contains a 15-pixel gap, while the product spacing scale contains:

```
12px
16px
20px
24px
```

The weak workflow says:

The design says 15, so use 15.

The stronger workflow asks:

- Was 15 intentional?
- Is it an unbound design value?
- Should the code use the existing 16-pixel token?
- Should the design be corrected?
- Does the component need a legitimate new spacing value?

MCP does not eliminate design-system decisions.

It reveals where those decisions are required.

## Phase 4: Implement the smallest vertical slice

Do not ask Claude to build an entire product flow in one action.

Start with one coherent slice:

- one page;
- one modal;
- one form;
- one card system;
- one responsive section;
- one state transition.

Example:

```
Implement only the order summary section from the linked Figma frame.
Requirements:
- Reuse the mapped repository components.
- Use existing design tokens.
- Use the original Figma assets.
- Preserve existing data and state-management patterns.
- Implement loading, empty, error, and populated states where the
 current product architecture already supports them.
- Do not modify unrelated files.
- Run type checking, linting, and relevant tests.
- Summarize every file changed and any unresolved discrepancy.
```

The goal is not merely to reduce risk.

Smaller steps make visual validation possible.

When five sections are wrong in different ways, it is difficult to determine whether the problem came from:

- bad design context;
- incorrect component mapping;
- CSS architecture;
- token mismatch;
- responsive assumptions;
- or an overly broad prompt.

## Phase 5: Validate the rendered interface

“Implementation complete” should never mean “the files were edited.”

The implementation must be rendered.

Ask Claude to:

1. start the application;
2. open the relevant route;
3. capture the rendered result;
4. compare it with the Figma screenshot;
5. list discrepancies;
6. correct them;
7. run validation again.

Example prompt:

```
Run the application and inspect the implemented page at:
/checkout
Compare the rendered interface against this Figma frame:
[Figma frame URL]
Evaluate:
- overall hierarchy;
- width and alignment;
- spacing;
- typography;
- component variants;
- borders and radii;
- icons and imagery;
- responsive behavior;
- loading, empty, error, disabled, hover, and focus states.
Do not say that it matches unless you have inspected both.
Fix the highest-impact differences first and report anything that
cannot be resolved without a product or design decision.
```

The phrase “do not say that it matches unless you have inspected both” matters.

AI agents tend to report completion based on code structure.

Designers care about rendered output.

Those are not the same thing.

## Phase 6: Send the live UI back to Figma

This is where the workflow becomes genuinely different.

Using Figma’s code-to-canvas capability, Claude Code can start the local application and capture the live interface into a new or existing Figma file as editable design layers.

Prompt:

```
Start the local application and capture the checkout flow into this
Figma file:
[Figma file URL]
Capture these states as separate frames:
1. Default checkout.
2. Validation errors.
3. Processing payment.
4. Payment success.
5. Payment failure.
6. Mobile viewport.
Use the Figma MCP code-to-canvas workflow.
```

Now the designer can review the real product states side by side.

This solves a common problem in product design:

The design file contains the ideal state.

The production interface contains reality.

Reality includes:

- long names;
- missing avatars;
- API errors;
- disabled actions;
- permissions;
- slow loading;
- overflowing content;
- unexpected combinations of states;
- real browser rendering.

Capturing the live product into Figma creates a canvas for reviewing reality rather than intention alone.

## Phase 7: Revise the canvas with Claude

The remote Figma MCP server can also write native Figma structures back to the canvas through `use_figma`. It can work with frames, components, variants, variables, Auto Layout, text, and other Figma objects.

A designer can ask:

```
Using this Figma file:
[Figma file URL]
Inspect the captured checkout error state.
Create two alternative layouts that:
- preserve the current design system;
- make the error more visible;
- keep the primary action available;
- work at mobile width;
- use existing components and variables;
- use Auto Layout throughout.
Place the alternatives on a new page called "Checkout Error Exploration".
Do not change the approved production frames.
```

This is not necessarily how final design judgment should be made.

But it is useful for:

- producing state variations;
- reorganizing large flows;
- applying variables;
- generating component variants;
- constructing exploration pages;
- fixing repetitive Auto Layout issues;
- creating structured review material.

The output remains editable Figma content rather than a generated image.

## Phase 8: Feed the approved revision back into code

Once the designer approves a revision, send the exact frame or selection link back to Claude Code.

```
The approved revision is here:
[Figma frame URL]
Compare it with the current implementation.
Before editing:
1. List the visual and behavioral changes.
2. Identify which changes affect shared components.
3. Identify which changes are page-specific.
4. Identify whether any new token or component variant is required.
Then implement only the approved differences.
Run the page, compare it again, and report remaining discrepancies.
```

That completes the loop:

```
Figma intent
 ↓
Code implementation
 ↓
Running interface
 ↓
Captured Figma review
 ↓
Approved revision
 ↓
Updated implementation
```

This is the workflow that makes Claude Code + Figma MCP strategically important.

Not first-pass generation.

Iteration continuity.

## Part IV: The designer’s role changes

Figma MCP does not make the designer irrelevant.

It makes certain kinds of designer work more valuable and exposes the weakness of others.

## Less valuable: manually documenting obvious dimensions

A designer should not spend hours creating redline-style documentation for every gap, radius, and color when those properties already exist structurally in Figma.

The agent can retrieve them.

## More valuable: defining systems

The quality of the output increasingly depends on:

- component architecture;
- token discipline;
- semantic naming;
- variant logic;
- responsive rules;
- state coverage;
- accessibility intent;
- behavioral annotations.

A polished frame with no underlying system becomes less useful.

A well-structured design file becomes executable context.

## Less valuable: designing only the ideal state

A single pristine dashboard frame is not a complete design.

The agent and developer still need answers for:

- no data;
- partial data;
- maximum data;
- errors;
- permissions;
- latency;
- disabled controls;
- destructive confirmation;
- keyboard navigation;
- mobile layouts.

## More valuable: reviewing product reality

Once running UI can return to the canvas, the designer can focus more directly on:

- inconsistencies across real routes;
- edge-case failures;
- system drift;
- copy problems;
- density;
- hierarchy;
- interaction quality;
- accessibility;
- product coherence.

The designer moves from preparing isolated pictures to supervising a living interface system.

## Part V: High-value workflows beyond design-to-code

## 1\. Design-system auditing

Ask Claude to compare a product screen with available design libraries and repository components.

```
Audit this Figma page and the corresponding implementation.
Identify:
- detached or recreated components;
- raw values that should use variables;
- components with inconsistent variants;
- duplicate code components;
- Figma components without code mappings;
- code components without a clear Figma equivalent;
- missing or outdated Code Connect mappings.
Return a prioritized cleanup plan.
```

This is one of the strongest use cases because design-system inconsistency is usually distributed across two different environments.

MCP gives the agent visibility into both.

## 2\. Component mapping with Code Connect

Code Connect is especially valuable for frequently reused primitives:

- buttons;
- fields;
- selects;
- cards;
- navigation;
- alerts;
- modals;
- tables;
- tabs;
- badges;
- typography;
- icons.

Figma recommends connecting core, frequently used components first, adding implementation instructions, and keeping mappings updated as component APIs change.

Do not start by mapping every decorative component in the library.

Map the components that control the largest amount of implementation behavior.

## 3\. Responsive design validation

Give Claude:

- the desktop Figma frame;
- the mobile frame, when available;
- the existing responsive code;
- the relevant container and breakpoint rules.

Then ask it to explain the transformation between the two.

```
Compare these desktop and mobile Figma frames:
[Desktop URL]
[Mobile URL]
Describe the responsive behavior as rules rather than screenshots:
- stacking changes;
- order changes;
- hidden or collapsed elements;
- container-width changes;
- typography changes;
- spacing changes;
- navigation changes;
- table or card transformations.
Then compare those rules with the existing implementation.
Do not edit files yet.
```

This encourages Claude to infer a responsive system rather than generate two unrelated layouts.

## 4\. Edge-state generation

Once the base component system exists, Claude can help construct neglected states in Figma:

- empty;
- loading;
- error;
- offline;
- locked;
- expired;
- permission denied;
- partial completion;
- oversized content.

The designer should still review relevance and hierarchy.

But the repetitive structural work can be delegated.

## 5\. FigJam flows from the codebase

The Figma MCP server can generate editable FigJam diagrams from natural language or Mermaid-style structure, including flowcharts, state diagrams, sequence diagrams, architecture diagrams, and entity-relationship diagrams.

A useful prompt:

```
Inspect the authentication implementation in this repository.
Generate a FigJam state diagram showing:
- signed out;
- password entry;
- MFA challenge;
- invalid MFA;
- password reset;
- session expiration;
- locked account;
- authenticated state.
Use the Figma MCP generate_diagram tool.
```

This gives designers a view of flows that may exist in code but never made it into the original design documentation.

## Part VI: Common mistakes

## Mistake 1: Treating the Figma URL as the entire brief

The frame does not necessarily contain:

- product requirements;
- business rules;
- analytics requirements;
- validation logic;
- permissions;
- accessibility behavior;
- technical constraints.

MCP provides design context.

It does not automatically provide every form of context.

## Mistake 2: Asking for the whole application

Large requests produce large assumptions.

Break work into:

1. inspection;
2. mapping;
3. implementation plan;
4. one vertical slice;
5. validation;
6. iteration.

Figma also recommends making large write-to-canvas changes incrementally: inspect first, then update variables, components, and layouts in smaller validated steps.

## Mistake 3: Skipping the screenshot

Structured data explains how the frame is built.

The screenshot shows how it actually looks.

Use both.

## Mistake 4: Letting Claude invent assets

Do not accept:

- substitute icons;
- random icon packages;
- gradient placeholders;
- generated stock imagery;
- generic illustrations.

Figma MCP provides asset download capabilities for exports and original source images. It also distinguishes between screenshots used for visual inspection and assets intended for export or transfer.

## Mistake 5: Assuming exact pixels are always correct

The design may contain:

- accidental values;
- detached instances;
- inconsistent spacing;
- unbound colors;
- outdated components.

Visual fidelity matters.

System fidelity matters more over time.

The agent should report conflicts instead of silently hard-coding them.

## Mistake 6: Trusting “done”

Completion should require evidence:

- the project runs;
- the route renders;
- types pass;
- lint passes;
- tests pass;
- the implementation was visually inspected;
- key states were reviewed;
- discrepancies were reported.

An agent saying “implemented successfully” is not evidence.

## Part VII: Current limitations

This workflow is powerful, but it is not fully autonomous.

Figma currently describes write-to-canvas as a beta-level capability that still requires manual review. Its documented limitations include per-call output constraints, unsupported custom fonts, and limitations around assets inside the write-to-canvas path. Components may also require manual publication before Code Connect workflows are complete.

The broader MCP server does provide separate tools for asset download and upload, but that does not mean every asset-heavy generation request will work perfectly inside a single canvas-writing operation.

You should also expect failure around:

- extremely large frames;
- poorly named layers;
- complex prototype logic;
- inconsistent design systems;
- unusual font setups;
- undocumented responsive behavior;
- ambiguous component mappings;
- outdated design files;
- codebases with no stable architecture.

The tool can reduce translation work.

It cannot compensate indefinitely for missing decisions.

## The real transformation

The obvious interpretation of Claude Code + Figma MCP is:

Designers can generate frontend code.

That is true, but strategically shallow.

The more important transformation is that the border between design and implementation becomes permeable.

Design files can inform code.

Code can return to the canvas.

Production components can be mapped to design components.

Live states can become reviewable design material.

Design revisions can return to the same implementation context.

The handoff does not disappear because Claude writes code.

The handoff disappears when design and implementation stop being separate packets of information.

That requires more than connecting an MCP server.

It requires:

- structured Figma files;
- a disciplined component library;
- shared tokens;
- Code Connect mappings;
- repository-level instructions;
- small implementation steps;
- rendered validation;
- continuous reconciliation.

Without those things, Claude Code becomes a faster way to produce inconsistent frontend code.

With them, it becomes part of a design operating system.

And that is the real opportunity.

Not replacing designers.

Not replacing developers.

Replacing the repeated loss of context between them.

## Practical workflow checklist

Before implementation:

- Connect the remote Figma MCP server.
- Confirm authentication through `/mcp`.
- Clean component and layer names.
- Apply Auto Layout and variables.
- Identify the source of truth.
- Add repository rules to `CLAUDE.md`.
- Configure Code Connect for high-value components.

During implementation:

- Ask Claude to inspect before editing.
- Map Figma elements to repository components.
- Resolve token conflicts.
- Implement one vertical slice.
- Use exact Figma assets.
- Preserve repository architecture.
- Run the application.

During review:

- Compare rendered UI with Figma.
- Review responsive and edge states.
- Capture the live UI back into Figma.
- Make revisions as structured canvas content.
- Send the approved frame back to Claude.
- Revalidate after implementation.

The best prompt is not the one that generates the most code.

It is the one that leaves the fewest important decisions hidden.
